To fix (3)

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 1 imprecise p value out of 21 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
p < .05 One experiment (Lambrechts et al., 2013, Experiment 1) stays time over space, because the rule uses the authors’ uncorrected p < .05 and not their Bonferroni threshold.

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

Let F(x) = E[logistic(Kx)] for a non-negative, almost surely finite sharpness K with one distribution for every pair, and H = logit F. For 0 < t < 1, odds compression φ_t(p) = logistic(t logit p) is convex on [1/2, 1), since φ_t″/φ_t′ = [(2p -1) -t(2φ_t -1)] / (p(1 -p)) with 1/2 ≤ φ_t ≤ p.

To check (5)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 14 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = .95 The permutation control is non-discriminating (p = .95): time takes 112 of 121 column votes, so shuffled data are as triangular as the real data.
p = .081 Before the recode the registered test gave 26 against 14, p = .081.
p = .108 Among the 39 directional experiments the share coded space over time was .64, 95% interval [.47, .79], and the registered two-sided exact sign test, reported as descriptive, does not reject equality, p = .108.
p = .058 The registered secondary analysis of the adult visual subset gives 23 against 11 (.68, 95% interval [.49, .83], p = .058), not significant at .05, or 24 against 11 (p = .041) if one disputed experiment (Reali et al., 2019) is coded space over time.
p = .38 The registered paper-level tally gives 13 papers against 8 (.62, 95% interval [.38, .82], p = .38).
p = .19 An ordinal mixed model with a random intercept per paper (61 experiments, 38 papers) puts the latent center 0.53 logits toward space over time, SE = 0.41, p = .19.
p = .26 A sign-flip test that flips every experiment of a paper together gives p = .26 (Appendix B).
p = .108 Sign test of 25 against 14: p = .108 (two-sided).
p = .54 Logical dependence (a possibility Garner, 1976, p. 102, left open; the rule for sentences and definitions is ours). Everything that exists has a time, and most things that have a size or color have a place. A rule that states the dependent dimension under the one it depends on produces the dictionary matrix without any conceptual hierarchy, and it licenses 117 of the 121 directional senses. A registered coding by this rule, with coders shown the whole sentence, supported dependence but could not fail, because the question it asked was set by the direction (deposit, dependence/adversarial/). After the registered analyses we replaced it: coders shown only the thing located and the two expressions marked which, if either, needs the other. Of the 243 directional English and Indonesian sentences (pairings, unweighted), a place was stated at a time in 121 of 134 where the place needs the time (0.90), in 37 of 53 where each needs the other (0.70) and in 32 of 47 where neither needs the other (0.68, 95% interval 0.53 to 0.81). The 9 pairings where the time needs the place are too few to read (5 of 9). Dependence raises that share in English (odds ratio 8.9, place-needs-time pairings against those where the time needs the place or neither needs the other) but hardly in Indonesian (1.7, p = .54). The two languages differ (p = .04), so the pooled odds ratio of 3.9 (Mantel-Haenszel, stratified by language) is an average. Where neither needs the other, time still comes first in both languages: 13 of 20 English pairings (0.66 weighted to the corpus, 95% interval 0.42 to 0.88) and 19 of 27 Indonesian ones (0.70, 0.50 to 0.86). Neither interval excludes one half, so this post hoc coding, which judges need between the two stated expressions, leans against dependence without ruling it out. Navon saw part of the dependence account: the reverse occupancy statement, with time stated at a place, “would have been equally logical” (p. 227), so for him the asymmetry was not logic alone, though on the same page he derives “here” from “now”. Beyond the post hoc dependence coding, the two accounts predict opposite orders only on pairs where the dimension that depends on the other sits higher in the hierarchy, or on the chaining of pairs (Appendix D.3). None of the four registered studies tests those pairs or that chaining. Figure 7 draws the three cases.
p = .108 That point is not a second estimate of the same gap, and its own direction is uncertain (registered two-sided p = .108).
p = .108 The registered two-sided test gives p = .108 and does not reject.
p = .108 Sign test of 25 against 14: p = .108 (two-sided).
p = .108 items putting the first over the second share = logistic(gap) text, scope criterion: time over place 0.738 (95% interval 0.561 to 0.893) interference experiments: time over space 14 of 39 (direction uncertain, p = .108; one scale would need a negative gap)The share follows the gap Intuition figure.
p = .108 That point is not a second estimate of the same gap, and its own direction is uncertain (registered two-sided p = .108).

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

To check Codebook Check

What we found

  • We parsed 5 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
  • 3 of 638 data columns (0%) are documented in a codebook; 635 are not.
  • A codebook was found and parsed (5 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents TP, PT, PAR while the data has item, class, reason. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.
Show details

For example, the codebook documents TP, PT, PAR while the data has item, class, reason. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. Documented but Unused Variables

5 documented variables were not matched to any data column.

Variable Label Source
TP The sentence states where something is (a location, position, or place reached as a state), and a time expression restricts when that holds. p65_codebook-v2-sec2.md
PT The sentence states a time value (clock time, date, season, timing of an event), and a place expression restricts where that holds. p65_codebook-v2-sec2.md
PAR Time and place each locate an event or action; neither restricts the truth of the other. p65_codebook-v2-sec2.md
AMB Time and place are both present and literal, but the coder cannot choose between TP, PT and PAR, even with the previous sentence. p65_codebook-v2-sec2.md
NA No literal time expression, or no literal place expression, or one is figurative or institutional. p65_codebook-v2-sec2.md

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 13 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 638 columns across 127 data files.

Issues Identified

22 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 127 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Reproducibility Check

Ethics Approval Check

We did not detect an ethics approval statement, and this paper does not appear to involve live data collection from human or animal participants. Ethics approval is typically not required for theoretical work, simulations, reviews, meta-analyses, or secondary analyses of published data.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
