3. The dictionary study: verbs of change in three dictionaries

3.1 Method Navon (p. 226) observed that verbs of change such as grow, mature and fade (change verbs, from here on) are always read as changes over time, so much so that Webster's definitions of "to fade" do not even mention time; that fewer verbs (shade, slope) describe changes over space; and that he had "not found any verb that could be interpreted to denote changes of time or space as a function of some other dimensions". His source, the 1973 edition of Webster's New Collegiate Dictionary, is not held. We tested the claim on three openly licensed dictionaries: WordNet 3.1 (Miller, 1995; Princeton University, 2010; 13,789 verb synsets), Webster's Revised Unabridged 1913 as distributed in GCIDE 0.53 (GNU Project, 2021; 25,354 verb definitions), and English Wiktionary (91,176 verb senses, kaikki.org extract of 2026-10-31; Ylonen, 2022). The registration, with checksums, the frozen codebook and the analysis rules, was committed before any item was drawn (commit ea3fef9).

For each sense, a coder read the definition only and recorded three things: whether it describes a change, which dimension changes (time, position (space), size, color, intensity, quantity, other), and what the change is described as varying over (the same dimensions, or items, or unspecified). Here "over" follows Navon's usage: the changing dimension varies over the dominant one, so "color changes over time" means time dominates color. The dominant dimension comes second here, where the corpus study's label "time over place" names it first. We kept Navon's own reading rule: a change sense that names no dimension counts beside "over time", never pooled with it silently. A falsifier is a sense in which time changes over another dimension, on both coders.

Four strata were drawn per dictionary: 150 random senses matching a change-word filter, a full census of every verb sense containing a time word with a change or variation word (580 real senses), every sense of Navon's six example verbs, and 200 random senses with no filter. Five fabricated senses in which time changes over space were planted in the census as a negative control. In all, 1,725 items were shuffled and shown without dictionary or stratum. Two AI coders coded them blind, and a third settled the 141 disagreements.

An independent verification by separate code reproduced every count, re-downloaded the dictionaries against their checksums, and ran a second recall sweep by a different regular expression over all 130,319 verb senses.

3.2 Results

Agreement was high: Cohen's kappa 0.91 for whether a sense is a change (n = 1,725), 0.95 for which dimension changes and 0.89 for what it changes over (n = 931 senses both coders called a change). All five plants were flagged by both coders.

Most change senses name no dimension at all ("to become X"), which Navon read as implicit change over time: 96% of change senses in the unfiltered WordNet sample (66 of 69), 98% in Webster's 1913 (58 of 59) and 93% in Wiktionary (65 of 70). Of the change senses in the two random strata (neither selected on a time word) that say what they vary over, 23 of 27 vary over time (95% interval 0.68 to 0.94). Adding the census of time-word senses, which is selected on time words and so cannot stand for dictionary senses in general, gives 105 of 113. The senses of Navon's six example verbs bring the pool to 112 of 121. Figure 3 shows the pooled matrix.

One sense in the three dictionaries describes time varying over another dimension: Wiktionary's time-change, "to undergo a difference in clocktime between two or more different time zones". It is tagged uncommon, and the entry still carries an open request for an attested example. A second candidate, Webster's soil ("light colors soil sooner than dark ones"), reached only two of three coders. Under the registered both-coder rule, Navon's report of no such verb therefore holds for WordNet and Webster's 1913 (soil enters the matrix on the adjudicated code, not the falsifier count) and fails in Wiktionary only on that single unattested sense.

The registered falsifier covers time only. For space, refract is the one candidate. The second recall sweep, by a different route, found no further candidate in any of the three dictionaries. Two independent searches and a reading of every hit support that absence but are not a full census, so the result shows that such senses are rare rather than absent.

On the registered shape prediction (Appendix D.7, prediction F5), the matrix is near-triangular in Navon's t im e s p a c e s iz e c o lo r in t e n s it y q u a n t it y o t h e r ... changes over this dimension time space size color intensity quantity other this dimension ...

Final codes (two coders, third adjudicates) from change-verbs/codes/; plants excluded; darker cell = more senses (steps 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64). hierarchy: of 121 directional votes, Navon's hierarchy misplaces 3 (2.5%). The prediction nonetheless fails as registered, because the falsifier count is not zero and an order in which "other" dominates space does strictly better, by one item (refract, coded as direction changing over density on two of three coders). The permutation control is non-discriminating (p = .95): time takes 112 of 121 column votes, so shuffled data are as triangular as the real data. The near-triangular shape follows from the column margin. Nearly everything changes over time, and the matrix says nothing finer about an order among the other dimensions. Transitivity and additivity are not testable here: no pair without time holds more than three votes, too few to settle a direction, and a pair with no votes in one direction has no finite logit. Garner (1976, pp. 102, 105) left open whether such asymmetries reflect processing level or inherent logical relations between dimensions. The second reading, extended here from perception to definitions, is the rival. Because nearly every directional sense runs over time, these data fit the rival (117 of 121 directional senses are changes on a dimension that logically needs the one it varies over, by the registered dependence table, deposit file p65_change-verbs-registration_2026-11-14.md) as well as Navon's hierarchy. The change criterion in dictionaries cannot tell a conceptual hierarchy from logical dependence.

4. The interference study: published interference experiments as tests of the interference criterion

Navon cited Garner's (1976) test as evidence of dominance in processing: if variation on one dimension slows sorting by a second, but variation on the second does not slow sorting by the first, the interfering dimension dominates (p. 223). We extend that test from sorting speed to biased magnitude judgments, which is what the space-time literature measures. Here space is spatial extent, length or distance, where the corpus study coded location. Many experiments, most of them since Casasanto and Boroditsky (2008), have measured such interference for space and time, in both directions and in the same participants. We registered a coding and counting rule before searching (commit 66d9131) and coded every such experiment we could find. The search, in November 2026, covered the works OpenAlex lists as citing key experiments (Casasanto & Boroditsky, 2008; Cai & Connell, 2015; Merritt et al., 2010) and one review, web searches, and the reference lists of the papers read. Two earlier narrative reviews cover the same asymmetry (Marcos & Genovesio, 2017; Loeffler et al., 2018).

Sixty-four experiments from 39 papers qualified, all read in full. Ten papers first coded from their abstracts were recoded from the full text after the result was known (deposit file p65_armC_fulltext-recode_com-parison_2026-11-19.md). Before the recode the registered test gave 26 against 14, p = .081. Appendix E lists every paper with its codes. Most were designed to test the metaphor account (Casasanto & Boroditsky, 2008; Casasanto, Fotakopoulou, & Boroditsky, 2010; Merritt, Casasanto, & Brannon, 2010), which predicts space interfering with time, so the published record is not a neutral sample of possible designs. Only the effect of space on time reached significance in 25, only that of time on space in 14, and both in 22 (coded symmetric; neither in 3 more). Among the 39 directional experiments the share coded space over time was .64, 95% interval [.47, .79], and the registered two-sided exact sign test, reported as descriptive, does not reject equality, p = .108. Counting significant results (vote counting) ignores effect sizes and power, and treats experiments from the same paper as independent. The registered secondary analysis of the adult visual subset gives 23 against 11 (.68, 95% interval [.49, .83], p = .058), not significant at .05, or 24 against 11 (p = .041) if one disputed experiment (Reali et al., 2019) is coded space over time. Three further analyses respect the clustering of experiments within papers. The registered paper-level tally gives 13 papers against 8 (.62, 95% interval [.38, .82], p = .38). Two exploratory analyses, added after the result, keep the 22 experiments in which both effects reached significance. An ordinal mixed model with a random intercept per paper (61 experiments, 38 papers) puts the latent center 0.53 logits toward space over time, SE = 0.41, p = .19. A sign-flip test that flips every experiment of a paper together gives p = .26 (Appendix B). Nine experiments reported slopes on a common scale. Their random-effects mean asymmetry is small and does not differ from zero (+0.018 of the stimulus range, 95% interval -0.002 to +0.037), with large heterogeneity between experiments. A control that shuffled direction labels within experiments returned no asymmetry, as it must.

Figure 4 shows the tally by direction and participant group, and the nine effect sizes.

61 rows both reached). Two of its three substantive disagreements were ruled by the registered rule. One experiment (Lambrechts et al., 2013, Experiment 1) stays time over space, because the rule uses the authors' uncorrected p < .05 and not their Bonferroni threshold. The other (Riedl & Hallez, 2026, Experiment 1) was coded from the abstract by the second coder and from the full text by the first, and the full-text code stands: both visual main effects are significant and the authors report no direction test, which the registered rule codes as symmetric. The second coder's own codes give 27 against 13 (p = .038), so the direction agrees across coders but the significance decision does not. The third is Reali et al. (2019), coded space over time from its abstract and by the second coder, and symmetric in the full-text recode, a ruling we made after seeing both codes because the registered rule does not decide it. The second coder's tally is not significant when counting papers or its full-text rows only. The codes rest on reported significance patterns, not on tests of the difference between the two effects, so a vote records which effect reached significance, not which was larger. The tally describes the published record. Only the nine slope experiments give a direct contrast.

By the interference criterion, the published experiments do not show time dominating space. If anything they lean toward space dominating time. The direction depends on the paradigm: moving or growing visual stimuli give space over time (Casasanto & Boroditsky, 2008; Starr & Brannon, 2016), as do static lines in adults (Merritt et al., 2010), while touch (Cai & Connell, 2015), harder spatial tasks (Vidaud-Laperrière et al., 2022, Experiment 2; Homma & Ashida, 2019), evidence accumulated over time (Lambrechts et al., 2013; Martin et al., 2017) and repeated intervals (Pierson & Hallez, 2026, within one experiment coded equal overall) give time over space. Visual size illusions give equal interference (Bratzke, 2024; Bratzke et al., 2024), and navigation in virtual reality gives equal interference in one study (Riemer et al., 2022) and space over time in another (Riemer et al., 2018). In moving and growing stimuli, speed ties length to duration, and speed can produce the space-over-time lean (Riemer et al., 2026). Navon anticipated that interference might not follow his hierarchy: the conceptual hierarchy, he wrote, need not match priority in attention and memory (p. 227).

5. The error study: slips, learners' errors and language disorders

People's errors are a second, non-experimental record of how they hold time and space apart. We mapped 33 published sources on slips of the tongue and pen, learners' errors, child language, language disorders, spatial neglect, gesture, brain imaging and language change (28 read in full and 1 in part, the rest as abstracts or as cited). Ten show space dominating time, six show the two coming apart (one source counts in both groups), seven are mixed, ten have no bearing on direction, one is not yet read, and none shows time dominating space. Two sources coded mixed partly support time dominating space: Feagans (1980) and Lafford and Ryan (1995), whose learners of Spanish used por for time at lower proficiency than for paths through space. The strongest cases are aphasic patients who lose spatial and temporal meanings of the same prepositions separately (Kemmerer, 2005; Mätzig, 2009, found no reliable spatial-temporal difference in five other patients), patients with spatial neglect who also neglect the "past" side of time (Saj et al., 2014), and Williams syndrome, where time acuity is spared while spatial acuity is impaired relative to verbally matched controls (Rousselle et al., 2013). Figure 5 maps the sources by direction code and shows the registered count described below. Errors bear mainly on the metaphor account. Neither Navon nor Garner states a prediction for them. We ran one registered count (commit 0c6fcdd) in 1.22 million words of learner English (the Cambridge First Certificate in English corpus, FCE, and the Write & Improve corpus; Yannakoudakis et al., 2011; Bryant et al., 2019). Only ten corrections crossed the time-space line, eight putting a time word where a place word belonged and two a place word where a time word belonged. The share of space-for-time errors was 0.20 (95% interval 0.03 to 0.56, inconclusive). Native writers in 23,117 words made none. Four of the eight time-for-space errors are "mentioned before" corrected to "mentioned above", a convention of written text rather than a confusion about physical space. Such errors are too rare in writing to decide anything. A count in the open Simon Fraser University Speech Error Database (SFUSED) is planned.

6. Discussion

>Discussion

6.1 The studies lean in different directions

The scope and change criteria put time first, and the interference test leans toward space first. The scope criterion puts time over place in about three of four directional English sentences, and the point estimate favors time in every sample. The Indonesian census, below its registered yield of 100, agrees: 0.70 of its directional sentences put time over place, with an interval above one half. The change criterion puts time over nearly everything in dictionaries (112 of 121 directional senses), but so would any account on which everything that exists has a time. The interference criterion leans toward space dominating time: space interferes with time more often than time with space, though not significantly in the registered test. On a provisional coding, no source on slips of the tongue and pen, learners' errors or language disorders shows time dominating space, and Navon states no prediction about them.

Navon expected this possibility. "Different procedures may reveal different hierarchies, although the hope is that they will converge on just one" (p. 223).

On the present evidence the scope and change criteria and the interference criterion do not converge on time against space. Appendix D states what would settle it. One pair, time against place, has been measured under two criteria, scope in text and change in dictionaries (position there, 10 senses against 1), and both put time first. With one pair, a scale can test only which dimension comes first, so the only testable part of convergence is whether the criteria agree on that direction. Text settles its direction (lower bound 0.56 above one half). Interference does not settle its own direction, in the registered two-sided test or in a one-sided reading derived after the result was known. The point estimates therefore point in opposite directions (text has time dominating place, interference has space dominating time), but the registered analyses do not establish that the two criteria order time and space oppositely in the population. Figure 6 sets the five estimates on one axis. 0 .25 .5 .75 1 share putting time first, with 95% interval (document resample, logit, Wilson, or exact binomial, as in Sections 2 to 4) time first space or place first Interference criterion: slowing in experiments Change criterion: change in definitions Scope criterion: location in text English sentences (registered extension) 0.74 (0.56 to 0.89) 155 directional sentences, share weighted to the corpus Indonesian sentences (census) 0.70 (0.58 to 0.80) 49 of 70 directional sentences Dictionary senses (two random samples) 0.85 (0.68 to 0.94) 23 of 27 senses that name what they change over Experiments 0.36 (0.21 to 0.53) Each row is one criterion and sample, with its 95% interval and count: blue circles for the scope and change criteria, orange squares for the interference criterion by experiment and by paper. The dictionary row sets time against every other dimension, not place alone. The three scope and change intervals lie above the 0.5 line, and both interference intervals include it.

6.2 Three readings

Three accounts fit these results to different degrees.

Navon's hierarchy. The scope and change criteria both agree with it. The dictionaries show the change pattern Navon described, with a single unattested exception, and the corpus adds a new result in which time takes scope over place. Against it stands the interference criterion (p. 223), which he also warned might not match the conceptual hierarchy.

Logical dependence (a possibility Garner, 1976, p. 102, left open; the rule for sentences and definitions is ours). Everything that exists has a time, and most things that have a size or color have a place. A rule that states the dependent dimension under the one it depends on produces the dictionary matrix without any conceptual hierarchy, and it licenses 117 of the 121 directional senses. A registered coding by this rule, with coders shown the whole sentence, supported dependence but could not fail, because the question it asked was set by the direction (deposit, dependence/adversarial/). After the registered analyses we replaced it: coders shown only the thing located and the two expressions marked which, if either, needs the other. Of the 243 directional English and Indonesian sentences (pairings, unweighted), a place was stated at a time in 121 of 134 where the place needs the time (0.90), in 37 of 53 where each needs the other (0.70) and in 32 of 47 where neither needs the other (0.68, 95% interval 0.53 to 0.81). The 9 pairings where the time needs the place are too few to read (5 of 9). Dependence raises that share in English (odds ratio 8.9, place-needs-time pairings against those where the time needs the place or neither needs the other) but hardly in Indonesian (1.7, p = .54). The two languages differ (p = .04), so the pooled odds ratio of 3.9 (Mantel-Haenszel, stratified by language) is an average. Where neither needs the other, time still comes first in both languages: 13 of 20 English pairings (0.66 weighted to the corpus, 95% interval 0.42 to 0.88) and 19 of 27 Indonesian ones (0.70, 0.50 to 0.86). Neither interval excludes one half, so this post hoc coding, which judges need between the two stated expressions, leans against dependence without ruling it out. Navon saw part of the dependence account: the reverse occupancy statement, with time stated at a place, "would have been equally logical" (p. 227), so for him the asymmetry was not logic alone, though on the same page he derives "here" from "now". Beyond the post hoc dependence coding, the two accounts predict opposite orders only on pairs where the dimension that depends on the other sits higher in the hierarchy, or on the chaining of pairs (Appendix D.3). None of the four registered studies tests those pairs or that chaining. Figure 7 draws the three cases. Navon's zenith example carries a confound: noon is defined by the sun's place. We tested Navon's prediction against that confound after the registered analyses, coding rules committed first, and replaced an earlier coding that let coders see which expression restricted the other. Coders shown only the two expressions marked a pairing definitional when convention or astronomy fixes one by the other, as a time zone fixes clock time. The 20 such pairings of 243 stated a place at a time less often than the others (12 of 20; odds ratio 0.32, 95% interval 0.12 to 0.85). The others stated a place at a time in 86% of the coded English pairings and 72% of the Indonesian, so definitional pairings do not produce the direction.

The metaphor account. Space structures time in interference tasks (Casasanto & Boroditsky, 2008) and in neglect (Saj et al., 2014). It makes no prediction about scope in sentences, so it is not contradicted by the corpus study. It predicts that errors will more often put a place word where a time word belonged. The error study's one registered count found 2 such errors among 10, too few to test that prediction.

The simplest summary is that the scope and change criteria measure which dimension a sentence or definition uses as the frame for the other, and the interference criterion may measure which representation working memory holds more precisely (Cai et al., 2018; Cai & Wang, 2022). Those are different questions, and on the present data their point estimates differ for time and space.

Most of the work below puts space first. In perception, people cannot ignore irrelevant spatial information when they judge duration, but they can ignore duration when they judge space (Casasanto & Boroditsky, 2008). Boroditsky (2000) found time structured by metaphorical mappings from space. Children show the same space-over-time asymmetry as adults (Casasanto et al., 2010). Across cultures, people construe time spatially, with the future in front or, in Aymara, behind (Núñez & Sweetser, 2006). Two sources loosely agree with Navon. Kant (1781/1855, Transcendental Aesthetic, § 7) made time the condition of all appearances and space that of outer appearances only. Readers of narratives build a representation ordered by time, even when the text tells events out of order (Claus & Kelter, 2006). Tulving (2002) makes subjective time part of episodic memory, whereas for Eichenbaum (2014) hippocampal time cells add a dimension to spatial mapping. Most of these sources mean a different kind of priority from Navon's, and the studies here suggest that the answer depends on the kind.

6.3 What the scale model adds

Appendix D states Navon's hierarchy as one score per dimension, with the share of directional items a logistic function of the gap between two scores. In words: the wider the gap between two dimensions' scores, the more often the higher one is stated over the lower one. This is the Bradley-Terry model of paired comparisons (Bradley & Terry, 1952). Three consequences shape the future studies. A single scale implies transitivity, because the gap from the top dimension to the bottom one is the sum of two non-negative gaps (Proposition D.5). So an intransitive triad would refute every scale model at once, and a transitive one confirms little. For a complete table of shares strictly between 0 and 1, additivity of gaps on the logit scale is equivalent to the model, because each logit is a difference of two scores (Proposition D.6). So it is the sharp test of the Bradley-Terry scale against the pair-by-pair rival. A failure would reject that scale under the pooling and coder-error assumptions, not an ordinal hierarchy. Coder error at one rate on every pair biases the test toward the rival unless the error rate enters the likelihood, because flipping a fixed share of directions pulls every share toward one half, the far pair most (Proposition D.7). If some dimension is stated under others but never over any, as three dimensions are in the pooled dictionary matrix, the model's estimate does not exist, because lowering that dimension's score always raises the likelihood (Proposition D.3). A registration must therefore include a weak prior or a bias-reduced estimate and report a lower bound on the gap. The power table in Appendix D.6 gives the item counts each test needs.

6.4 Limitations

Two treebanks are not a balanced sample of English. Every coder in every study was an AI model, and no human coded any item. The two coders are AI models of one family (Claude Opus and Claude Sonnet), so a bias they share would not show up as disagreement, and their agreement (kappa 0.79 and 0.68 on the two registered corpus samples, 0.58 on the exploratory one) shows that they code consistently, not that their codes are right. A human coding of 300 of the same sentences is planned. The two post hoc codings of Section 6.2 used time and place expressions extracted by a model that read each sentence, so wording may carry the direction, and 50 rows with competing expressions were not audited. The corpus estimate rests on 155 directional sentences from a stratified draw with a design effect of about 6, so it carries the information of about 22 to 31 independent items. Dictionary definitions are lexicographers' paraphrases rather than usage. In 915 corpus uses of the dictionary study's change verbs, coders judged 3 of the 499 changes to run over space (0.6%), fewer than the dictionaries' 9 of 121 senses not over time (7.4%, p < .001, the registered comparison) and their 6 of 121 over space (5.0%, p = .002), so usage is no more spatial than the dictionaries for these verbs. Spatial-extent verbs such as "widen" and "slope" were not on that list, so an under-count for them is untested. Wiktionary repeats a Webster 1913 definition word for word in 4% of its verb senses (without them, 111 of 120 directional senses vary over time), so the three dictionaries are not fully independent. The interference tally counts experiments of unequal size and design as one vote each.

Its 64 experiments come from 39 papers and share laboratories, stimuli and often participants. Section 4 gives the registered paper-level tally and two exploratory clustered analyses. Each vote records a reported significance pattern, not a test of the difference (Section 4), and the slope difference treats the two slopes as independent. Four of the 33 error-map sources were read only as abstracts or as cited. Two languages are not many, and a language that folds time and place into one case ending has not been tested. The 500 Indonesian pilot sentences were coded under the first version of the language notes, whose pair-label agreement was low, and across the whole census the pair-label agreement was 0.60, at the registered bar and not above it. The orderliness criterion has no corpus form and needs a short judgment task.

6.5 Future studies

Two future studies are registered and frozen. The first has run only its pilots. The second has run its first language, Indonesian (Section 2.6), and its other nine languages are still to come, with ChatGPT as a coder from a second model family, a deviation registered as the fourth amendment (19 November 2026, commit 6e672bc). Coder family therefore differs between Indonesian and the other nine languages. Both studies apply the scope criterion, the first also compares it with the change criterion, and neither applies the orderliness criterion. Two hypotheses from Sections 6.2 and 6.4 have tests under way: that the interference criterion may measure which representation working memory holds more precisely, tested by whether the dimension with more discriminable stimulus steps interferes more, and that dictionaries miss spatial-extent verbs such as "widen", tested on their corpus uses. A behavioral test of the first is being built: people reproduce the length or the duration of a line while the other varies, and the precision reading predicts that the dimension with finer steps intrudes more on judgments of the other.

The first future study: six dimensions in English. Navon's hierarchy makes predictions about every pair of dimensions crossing his three levels, and one pair cannot test a hierarchy. The registration (commits in the private repository, listed with their dates in the deposit, frozen 2026-11-16) re-codes the 4,000 drawn sentences on time, place, size, color, quantity and manner under a codebook extended to all 30 ordered pairs, and tests direction per pair, transitivity on each eligible triad, additivity against the coder-error-corrected likelihood, and the rank-one test of convergence with the dictionary study's matrix on the five dimensions the two studies share, once a pilot count shows items on each shared pair in both studies (the dictionary matrix is sparse off the time column, and the D.6 power rows assume a complete design). Appendix D.6 calculates how many items each test needs: about 37 directional items per pair for direction at a share of 0.74, about 110 per pair on each of a triad's three pairs for additivity, and at least 20 per pair per criterion for the rank test. Two pilot rounds showed that asking coders to inventory six dimensions at once lowers agreement on presence (time-place kappa 0.38 on 58 pilot sentences), and the registration includes the stopping rules that follow from that finding. Time against size is the pair to code first: the interference experiments also measure it, so, with the dictionaries, which already code size changing over time, it would be the first pair measured by the scope, change and interference criteria.

The second future study: more languages. The frozen registration (SHA-256 1c3e0fee…, deposit file wave3/FREEZE.txt) names Indonesian as the first of ten languages, and Section 2.6 reports its census (6,628 sentences, two treebanks, release 2.18). The registration expected about 164 directional items (113 at the lower feasibility estimate), and the census returned 70, under the 100 of its yield rule, so the English yield did not carry over. At a true share of 0.74 the two-sided test of equal rates has power 1.00 at 164 or 113 items, and keeps power 0.80 down to a true share of about 0.62 at 164 items (exact binomial; the frozen registration's normal approximation put that share at 0.60). With one added language the between-language spread of the time-place gap cannot be estimated reliably, so the cross-linguistic question stays open. Extending it to eight to twelve languages follows Appendix D.5: for the mean direction, eight languages of 50 directional items each suffice if languages differ in their time-place gap by a logit standard deviation of 0.5, and twelve of 100 give power 0.90 if they differ by 1.0. Estimating the spread itself needs about 100 items in each of eight languages. The set has no language of the Americas and no sub-Saharan language other than an English-lexified creole, so even its full result would be a claim about those languages and not about human languages in general.

6.6 Conclusion

People say the position of the sun varies with time, not that the time varies with the position of the sun, and Navon read that asymmetry as evidence that time dominates space in how we conceive the world. Public text and dictionaries show a frequency form of the asymmetry he described. By the scope criterion, in English sentences time restricts place about three times as often as place restricts time, and in Indonesian sentences about twice as often.

By the change criterion, change verbs that say what they vary over mostly vary over time. The published interference experiments, read by the interference criterion, do not show time dominating space. So far the asymmetry is shown in sentences and definitions. The two future studies, across six dimensions and more languages, can sharpen but not settle the question of whether it also holds in how people represent time and space. A behavioral test of one of Navon's own criteria would bear on it directly. His third criterion, orderliness, is untested and suits such a test. A good first test applies it to time and position, with lights flashing at positions uncorrelated with time, Navon's own example (p. 225). code class definition anchor TP time over place The sentence states where something is (a location, position, or place reached as a state), and a time expression restricts when that holds. "The sun was overhead at noon." "By six the children were home." PT place over time The sentence states a time value (clock time, date, season, timing of an event), and a place expression restricts where that holds. "In Tokyo it was already midnight." "In Spain dinner is at ten." PAR parallel Time and place each locate an event or action; neither restricts the truth of the other. "We met in the park yesterday." "She flew here last night." AMB ambiguous Time and place are both present and literal, but the coder cannot choose between TP, PT and PAR, even with the previous sentence. "He was here then." NA not applicable No literal time expression, or no literal place expression, or one is figurative or institutional. "She came into office in 2004." (office = position) "Home in on the problem today." Decision steps for coders, in order: (1) literal time AND literal place present? If not, NA. (2) Is the sentence an event or action located in time and space? Then PAR. (3) Is a location state asserted, with time narrowing it? TP. (4) Is a time value asserted, with place narrowing it? PT. (5) Still torn: AMB.

Minimal pairs (the guide uses these): • "She was at the office on Monday." (location state at a time: TP) vs "She arrived at the office on Monday." (event: PAR) • "The train is in Boston at nine."

(TP) vs "It is nine o'clock in Boston." (PT) • "At noon the square is empty."

(TP) vs "Noon comes earlier in the eastern towns." (PT) Each coder also copies the time phrase and the place phrase (or leaves them blank for NA) and gives a confidence of 1 to 3. Two rules were added by the blind adjudicator in the later samples and adopted for the extensions: frequency words ("always", "never") are not literal time, and "when" and "while" clauses are.

Appendix B. Estimators and intervals

Corpus share (corpus study). The corpus was split into sampling cells (three in the first sample, six once the date-or-time screen split each group in two). Every sentence in a cell had the same chance of being drawn. The estimated number of sentences of a given class in the whole corpus is the sum over cells of the count coded in that cell, multiplied by the cell's population divided by its draw. The population is the cell's eligible sentences: 449 sentences over 60 tokens or containing offensive terms were excluded before sampling (registered protocol, section 4.4), leaving 30,526. The share of time over place is s = N_TP / (N_TP + N_PT), with N_TP and N_PT the estimated corpus counts of the two directional classes. The 95% interval resamples whole source documents within each cell, 10,000 times, because sentences from one document are not independent. It takes the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the resampled shares. The exploratory extension also reports a bracket: the share recomputed with the two newly sampled cells at the lower exact (Clopper-Pearson) bound for time over place and the upper bound for place over time, and again at the upper bound for time over place and the lower bound for place over time. A margin for coding errors follows from the weighted totals T (time over place) and P (place over time), as shares of all directional weight (T + P = 1). If at most E of the weight coded time over place is truly place over time, and coders missed at most M of place-over-time weight, the smallest true share is (T -E)/(T + P + M), which exceeds one half exactly when T -P > 2E + M (an argument from a ChatGPT review). At the registered share 0.738, T -P is 0.476 of the directional weight, so with M = 0 the point estimate stays above one half for E up to 0.237. A screen's recall for a direction is the estimated corpus count of flagged sentences of that class divided by the estimated count of all sentences of that class. Decision labels, from the lower bound L and upper bound U of that interval: L above 0.80 "supports the strong rate", L above 0.50 with U above 0.80 "supports direction", L above 0.50 with U below 0.80 "time dominates but below the strong rate", L at or below 0.50 with U at or above 0.50 "inconclusive", and U below 0.50 "against direction". The 0.80 threshold is a convention, not a value Navon states. A result is read as confirmatory only if Cohen's kappa between the two blind coders is at least 0.60, and exploratory otherwise. Fewer than 30 directional sentences means no directional test is run (outcome "insufficient"). Kappa intervals are bootstrap percentile intervals over sentences.

Dictionary counts (dictionary study).

Counts are of senses, de-duplicated across strata, with the five plants removed. Shares of a pair carry Wilson 95% intervals. The shape test fits every one of the 5,040 orders of the seven dimensions and scores each by the number of directional senses it misplaces, with a permutation control that shuffles the over-dimension across directional senses, 1,000 times, and drops shuffled pairs that land on the diagonal.

Interference tally (interference study).

Each experiment is one vote. The registered test is the two-sided exact sign test of space-over-time against time-over-space votes, with symmetric and null experiments set aside. A paper's vote is its majority code; 18 papers have no directional vote. The effect-size summary takes, per experiment, the difference between the two cross-dimension slopes expressed as a proportion of the stimulus range, with a standard error that treats the two slopes as independent, and pools them by the DerSimonian-Laird random-effects method. The control permutes the direction labels within experiments 10,000 times. Two exploratory analyses added after the registered test respect clustering by paper: a cumulative-logit mixed model with a random intercept per paper on the three-level code (time over space, symmetric, space over time; R package ordinal, adaptive quadrature), testing whether the two thresholds are centered on zero, and a sign-flip test that flips all of a paper's directional votes together (200,000 draws).

Learner errors (error study).

The registered quantity is the share of cross-domain preposition corrections that put a space word where a time word belonged, among all cross-domain corrections, with an exact 95% interval, read only if at least ten such corrections were found.

higher ones can be estimated rather than assumed away (Section D.4). Equation (D.1) is the Bradley-Terry model (Bradley & Terry, 1952) with strengths exp(k_c θ_d). The model adds a probabilistic scale to Navon's qualitative hierarchy: one set of scores, with θ_time > θ_place > every other θ, shared by every criterion, formalizes his hope that procedures converge (p. 223), and logistic additivity is a further modeling assumption of ours, not a claim of his. Figure D1 draws the scale. Top: only the time-minus-place gap is measured (1.04 logit units with the scope criterion's sharpness set to 1, from the corpus study's registered extension). Other positions are illustrative. Bottom: the measured text share 0.738 (95% interval 0.561 to 0.893, shaded) on the curve, and the interference experiments' 14 of 39 directional experiments placing time over space, which the same scale could fit only with a negative gap, or equivalently a negative sharpness for that criterion (Section D.4). That point is not a second estimate of the same gap, and its own direction is uncertain (registered two-sided p = .108). Model figure, Appendix D.1.

When counting only directional items is legitimate. Two facts justify conditioning on the directional items and setting the parallel class aside, under stated models. Whether parallel sentences and coding exclusions behave like such ties, and whether opportunities are direction-neutral (Remark D.1), is assumed, not shown. Davidson's (1970) model for ties, P(i over j) = π_i / (π_i + π_j + ν√(π_i π_j)), with the tie probability carrying the term ν√(π_i π_j). Conditional on a non-tie, P(i over j) = π_i / (π_i + π_j), which is exactly Bradley-Terry. Proof: the common denominator cancels in the ratio. Wolfram check W1 confirms the identity. Its control, the Rao-Kupper ties model (Rao & Kupper, 1967), fails the same identity unless π_i = π_j or its tie parameter is 1, which allows no ties (witness value 1/21), so the check can fail. PROVED. The lemma is sufficient for ignoring parallel items, not necessary. Under Rao-Kupper ties, ignoring them biases the scale.

Remark D.1 (how many items a pair yields).

The rate at which two dimensions co-occur is a property of the text, not of dominance. If the two directions of pair (i, j) are independent Poisson counts with means μ_ij exp(θ_i) and μ_ij exp(θ_j), the likelihood for θ given each pair's total is the binomial likelihood of (D.1). That likelihood is the standard log-linear form of Bradley-Terry (a standard result; no source was consulted for it here). So rare pairs give less information but no bias. The Poisson condition is sufficient, not necessary.

D.2 What the data identify Proposition D.2 (identification of the scale).

Within one criterion, with its sharpness k_c fixed at a nonzero value (Proposition D.4 removes this condition), the scores are identified up to an added constant if and only if the comparison graph is connected. The comparison graph has the dimensions as nodes, with an edge wherever a pair has at least one directional item.

Proof. If the graph is connected, every gap θ_i -θ_j is a sum of logits along a path, each identified from its pair's share, divided by the fixed sharpness k_c. If it is disconnected, adding a constant to every score in one component changes no probability. PROVED (necessary and sufficient).

Proposition D.3 (when the estimate exists).

Suppose the comparison graph is connected. Then a finite, unique maximum-likelihood estimate of the scores (with their sum fixed at zero) exists if and only if the win graph is strongly connected. The win graph has an arrow from i to j whenever i was stated over j at least once. This is Ford's (1957) partition assumption. The connectivity hypothesis matters. If the comparison graph is disconnected, finite maximizers can exist without a strongly connected win graph, but they are not unique (an independent verification found 15 such tables in 300). Necessity. If some set S of dimensions is never stated under the rest, raising every score in S increases the likelihood strictly, toward a supremum it never reaches, so no finite maximizer exists. Sufficiency. The log-likelihood is concave. Take any direction v that is not constant, within the sum-zero subspace, and let S be the set where v is largest. Strong connectivity gives some j outside S that was stated over some i in S. That item contributes log logistic(θ_j -θ_i), which tends to minus infinity along v. So the log-likelihood tends to minus infinity in every direction and attains its maximum. Connectivity of the comparison graph makes it strictly concave on the subspace, so the maximum is unique. Check A4 illustrates both sides: a strongly connected table gives finite scores, and a table where one dimension never loses drives its score to infinity. PROVED (necessary and sufficient, given a connected comparison graph).

Consequence. Navon reports finding no verb for time, or space, changing over another dimension (the change criterion; p. 226). If the data agree with him exactly, the estimate does not exist. That is not a defect of the data: the likelihood keeps rising as the gap grows, so no finite estimate exists. The six-dimension study must therefore register a weak prior or a bias-reduced estimate (for example a normal prior with standard deviation 3 on each score) and report the posterior lower bound on the gap, not a point estimate.

Proposition D.4 (several criteria). With criteria c = 1, …, C, each with a connected comparison graph, the products k_c(θ_i -θ_j) are identified. The products k_c θ_d themselves are not, because a shift of every score leaves every probability unchanged. So, if at least one criterion has nonzero sharpness and the scores are not all equal, (θ, k) is identified up to a shift of θ and a common rescaling (θ, k) → (θ/s, s k).

Fixing k at 1 for a criterion whose sharpness is not zero removes the scale. The ratios k_c / k_1 are identified only if the scores are not all equal. If every dimension ties, there is no hierarchy, and every sharpness k_c fits the data equally well. PROVED (connectivity within each criterion is sufficient here, and whether it is necessary is not shown; a design with missing pairs needs its own identification check).

D.3 Transitivity and additivity

Transitivity is a property any order must show. Additivity is the further property of the one-score model (Proposition D.6). They are the place where Navon's account and the logical-dependence rival part ways. On a logical-dependence reading (our construal of Garner, 1976, p. 102), asymmetries arise pair by pair, with no global score. That reading allows each pair its own direction and does not require the pairs to chain into one shared order.

Proposition D.5 (transitivity follows from any single scale).

Let the share be F(θ_i -θ_j) for any strictly increasing F with F(0) = 1/2. This covers Bradley-Terry, Thurstone's (1927) Case V, and every other model that ranks by one score. If P(i over j) ≥ 1/2 and P(j over k) ≥ 1/2, then P(i over k) ≥ max of the two. This is strong stochastic transitivity. Proof. The gap θ_i -θ_k is the sum of the two non-negative gaps, so it is at least each of them. F is increasing. PROVED. A single scale is sufficient for strong (and so weak) stochastic transitivity, not necessary. Some models with no scale are also transitive. So a transitive triad confirms little, and an intransitive one refutes every single-scale model at once.

Proposition D.6 (additivity characterizes Bradley-Terry).

For a complete table of shares strictly between 0 and 1, these three statements are equivalent: (i) the table is Bradley-Terry; (ii) logit P(i over k) = logit P(i over j) + logit P(j over k) for every triple; (iii) P_ij P_jk P_ki = P_ji P_kj P_ik for every triple (the product rule, which follows from the ratio form of Luce's choice axiom: Luce, 1959, as cited in Davidson, 1970, p. 319). Proof. (i)⇒(ii): each logit is a difference of scores, and the differences telescope (Wolfram W2).

(ii)⇒(i): fix a reference dimension r and set θ_i = logit P(i over r). Then logit P(i over j) = logit P(i over r) + logit P(r over j) = θ_i -θ_j. (ii)⇔(iii): take logs (W3). PROVED (necessary and sufficient).

Additivity is the sharp prediction (F3). If time over place and place over color are each 0.80, time over color must be 16/17 = 0.941 (exact, check A1). The logical-dependence rival, as constructed here with no chaining, allows 0.80. A dependence rival whose shares are near 0 or 1 saturates the logits and escapes this test. Additivity is specific to the logistic link. A Thurstone (probit) scale predicts 0.954 instead. Thurstone shares fail logit-additivity by 0.42 at gaps of 1 (W2 control). The two links differ by about 0.01 in share at the values seen here, so a rejection of (ii) well beyond 0.01 in share counts against a probit scale as well as the logistic one, though not against every increasing common link. Such a rejection can still arise from mixed sources (D.8) or coder error (D.7), and it does not reject an ordinal hierarchy, which transitivity alone tests (D.5).

Proposition D.7 (coder error makes a true scale look sub-additive). Suppose a coder reverses the direction of an item (codes i over j as j over i) with probability e < 1/2, independently of the item. The observed share is q = e + (1 -2e)P. Let g(x) = logit(e + (1 -2e) logistic(x)). Then g(0) = 0 and g is concave for x ≥ 0, so g(x + y) ≤ g(x) + g(y): the observed logit of the far pair falls short of the sum of the adjacent ones, with strict shortfall when 0 < e < 1/2 and both gaps are positive. These conditions are sufficient. Within non-negative gaps they are also necessary, since a zero gap gives equality. The proposition says nothing about gaps of opposite sign. Proof. Write s = logistic(x) and t = s -1/2. Then g'( x) is (1 -2e) times h(t) = (1/4 -t²) / (1/4 -a² t²), with a = 1 -2e. The derivative is h'(t) = 8(a² -1) t / (4a² t² -1)², which is ≤ 0 for0 ≤ t < 1/2 (Wolfram W4, which also refutes the opposite sign). Since t increases with x, g' decreases, so g is concave. A concave function with g(0) = 0 is subadditive on the non-negative half-line. PROVED. Figure D2 draws the effect.

Size of the effect. With e = 0.05, true shares 0.80, 0.80 and 0.941 are observed as 0.770, 0.770 and 0.897. Additivity applied to the observed adjacent shares predicts 0.918, so the far pair looks 0.25 logit short (checks A2, W4d). The power runs show what this does to a test. At 1,000 items per pair, a test that ignores coder error rejects a true scale 13% of the time instead of 5%. Including the known flip rate in the likelihood restores rejection to 4 to 6% (Section D.6). Consequence: any F3 test must estimate e, from validation labels or from double-coded items outside the triad under test, and put it in the likelihood. A flip rate fitted freely from the same three shares fits exactly any far-pair share above the larger adjacent share and up to the chained prediction (three parameters, three shares), so it absorbs the shortfall it should correct. Estimating e from disagreement assumes equal, independent, symmetric errors. A shortfall of the size above is otherwise what a true hierarchy plus ordinary coder noise produces. Such a shortfall would then be misread as support for the logical-dependence rival.

Proposition D.8 (pooling sources). Pooled shares mix sources: genres, criteria or languages. (a) If every source shares one order and differs only in sharpness, and the mix of sources is the same for every pair, strong stochastic transitivity survives. Both conditions are sufficient. Part (b) shows that without the common mix the conclusion can fail. Proof: each source term in P(i over k) is at least its term in P(i over j).

PROVED.

Additivity, in this case, holds as an inequality: the pooled logit is subadditive. Proof. Let F(x) = E[logistic(Kx)] for a non-negative, almost surely finite sharpness K with one distribution for every pair, and H = logit F. For 0 < t < 1, odds compression φ_t(p) = logistic(t logit p) is convex on [1/2, 1), since φ_t″/φ_t′ = [(2p -1) -t(2φ_t -1)] / (p(1 -p)) with 1/2 ≤ φ_t ≤ p. As logistic(tKx) = φ_t(logistic(Kx)), Jensen's inequality gives H(tx) ≥ tH(x); with t = x/(x + y) and t = y/(x + y), adding gives H(x + y) ≤ H(x) + H(y), strict unless a gap is zero or K is almost surely constant. The pooled logit need not be concave, so the argument uses this ratio property. PROVED (proof from a ChatGPT review, checked symbolically and on 5,000 random mixtures, and check A3c's 20,000 mixtures stand as numerical evidence). (b) If the mix differs by pair (time-place coded mostly from one genre, time-color from another), strong transitivity can fail while weak transitivity holds. Shares 0.993, 0.993 and 0.550 arise from one order with two sharpness values (check A3a). PROVED by example. (c) If sources hold different orders, the pooled table can cycle. Three equal sources with cyclic orders give two-thirds in every direction around the cycle (check A3b; the classical Condorcet construction). PROVED by example. Even so, any mixture of linear orders satisfies the triangle inequality P_ij + P_jk -P_ik ≤ 1. Proof: within one linear order the indicator sum [i>j] + [j>k] -[i>k] exceeds 1 only if i>j and j>k but not i>k, which transitivity forbids. A mixture averages the indicators. Every Bradley-Terry source is itself a mixture of linear orders (a random-utility model), so the bound covers mixtures of scales too. PROVED. The cyclic example gives 0.780 and 0.987 for source sharpness K = 2 and 5 (the K of part a) and approaches the bound of 1 as K grows (check A3b). A pooled table that breaks this bound cannot come from a mix of ordered sources with the same source weights on every pair. Common weights are sufficient for the bound. If pairs draw on the sources in different proportions, as when conditioning on directional items changes the mix, the bound can fail with every source ordered: two sources sharing one order, odds 9 and 1.1 per adjacent step, weighted 9 to 1 on the adjacent pairs and 1 to 9 on the far pair, give P_ij + P_jk -P_ik = 1.13. Weights are common to every pair exactly when directional yields factor into a source term and a pair term. The bound is the known triangle inequality for pairwise shares induced by a distribution over rankings. Fishburn (1990, p. 478) writes it as P_ij + P_jk ≥ P_ik, and reversing the labels gives the form used here.

Consequence.

Transitivity and additivity must be tested within one criterion and one language, or with the source in the model (Section D.5). A cycle in pooled data rules out one shared order. It does not rule out that every source has an order of its own. Figure D3 draws the three cases. Descriptive count. For the majority direction of each pair among D dimensions, the number of cyclic triads is the count of triples whose three majority directions form a cycle. Kendall and Babington Smith (1940) count such circular triads. When every pair has a majority direction (a sufficient condition: a tied pair leaves s_i undefined), the count also equals C(D,3) -Σ_i C(s_i, 2), with s_i the number of dimensions i beats.

The count is a description only. A cycle built from shares whose intervals span 1/2 is not evidence, so F2 keeps the registered rule: all three intervals clear of 1/2.

D.4 Do the criteria converge? A rank-one test, and its blind spot

Navon hoped that different procedures "will converge on just one" hierarchy (p. 223). In the model, this means one set of scores for every criterion, with only the sharpness allowed to differ.

Model.

Arrange the logits in a table with one row per pair and one column per criterion. Under (D.1) the entry is k_c(θ_i -θ_j), so the table has rank one: every column is a multiple of one column. The alternative fits a separate scale to each criterion.

Proposition D.9 (test statistic and degrees of freedom). The likelihood-ratio statistic G² = 2[ℓ(separate scale per criterion)ℓ(one scale, sharpness k_c)] has C(D -1) -[(D -1) + (C -1)] = (C -1)(D -2) degrees of freedom (Wolfram W5; the tempting (C -1)(D -1) fails, W5c). With six dimensions and three criteria, the test has 8 degrees of freedom. With two dimensions, it has none. PROVED (the count).

Null distribution.

G² is approximately chi-square on (C -1)(D -2) degrees of freedom when the true table has rank exactly one, every pair has enough items, and the sharpness of at least one criterion is not zero. These sufficient conditions are assumed here. The rank-zero simulation below shows that the last one cannot be dropped. That is CONDITIONAL on standard likelihood-ratio regularity, which is not re-proved here. Simulation agrees. With true rank one, D = 6, C = 3 and 60 items per pair per criterion, the mean G² was 8.16 against 8, and the test rejected 4.8% of the time at nominal 5% (check A5). With true rank zero (no hierarchy anywhere), the reference is wrong: mean 5.06, rejection 0.0%. The test is conservative there because the rank-one set has a corner at zero. NUMERICAL EVIDENCE. A parametric bootstrap from the fitted rank-one model is a candidate null distribution, but refitting alone does not calibrate it at or near a complete tie, where the fitted signal is itself noise-sized (in the two-by-two Gaussian analog the tie statistic has mean 2π/2, about 0.43, against 1 away from the tie, and a bootstrap from the fit inherits a random amplitude). The registration must check that regime by simulation. The chi-square value serves as a check.

Proposition D.10 (the blind spot).

A criterion that reverses every pair (k_c < 0, so that the lower-scored dimension of each pair is stated over the higher one) still gives a rank-one table. So the rank-one fit with sharpness of either sign, the fit used here, cannot see the one disagreement that matters most. A fit that forces k_c > 0 would reject a reversal, but it would then merge two questions, rank and sign, into one statistic. PROVED (k_c(θ_i -θ_j) is a multiple of the first column for any real k_c). In simulation, a full reversal was rejected 3 to 6% of the time, about the nominal rate, while the fitted k_c was negative in 100% of runs (check A6 and the power runs).

Restated prediction F4.

Navon's convergence, read as a shared scale under (D.1), is the conjunction of two conditions, each necessary, which are sufficient together. Agreement on Navon's order alone does not require rank one. The first is rank one (the G² test). The second is the same sign for every sharpness, k_c > 0, tested as F1 within each criterion. "Language favors time while interference favors space" looks like an example of rank-two structure. That example concerns the time-place pair only. With one pair the table has zero degrees of freedom, so only the sign of the disagreement is testable. Whether it is also a rank failure depends on the other pairs. If interference swapped the scores of time and place, putting place over time, it would be rank two (the "swap" scenario of D.6). If it reversed every pair, it would be rank one.

Where the data stand. Only time against place has been measured under two criteria, scope in text and change in dictionaries (position there), and both put time first. The experiments mostly measured a different kind of space (Section 4). One shared pair leaves zero degrees of freedom, so the rank test is not yet possible. The sign test is possible, because Navon claims time dominates every other dimension, extent included. Text (the scope criterion) puts time over place at 0.738, with a lower bound of 0.561, so its sign is settled. Interference experiments put time over space in 14 of 39 directional experiments. The registered two-sided test gives p = .108 and does not reject. Read one-sided against "interference also favors time", p is .054 (second coding: 13 of 40, two-sided .038, one-sided .019). Because text already favors time, the one-sided reading is the sign test for F4. That reading was derived after the interference-study result was known. It is therefore exploratory and does not override the registered two-sided result. It also treats each directional experiment as one directional item. Experiments differ in power and design, and the 22 experiments in which both effects reached significance drop out. The sign disagreement is OPEN: even that reading does not reject at .05 in the registered coding, though it does in the second coding.

D.5 Languages: how universal is the hierarchy?

Model. For language ℓ, θ(d, ℓ) = θ(d) + u(d, ℓ), u(d, ℓ) ~Normal(0, τ²), independent. (D.2)

In words: each language shifts each dimension's score by its own random amount. The standard deviation τ measures how far languages wander from a shared hierarchy. The model is a Bradley-Terry model with random effects, which is a binomial generalized linear mixed model. A constant added to every score in a language changes nothing, so only within-language gaps are identified. For one pair, the gap varies across languages with standard deviation s = τ√2.

Universality, three ways. 1. τ² itself. Zero means one hierarchy for all languages. 2. The share of score variance that is shared: ρ = Var(θ) / (Var(θ) + τ²). 3. The most readable: the chance that a new language keeps time over place, Φ((θ_time -θ_place) / s). At the English gap of 1.04 (logit of 0.738), s = 0.5 gives 0.98, and s = 1.0 gives 0.85.

Identification. τ is separable from binomial noise only with at least two languages, and in practice it needs many more. Testing τ = 0 puts the null on the edge of the parameter space. The likelihood-ratio reference is then an equal mixture of chi-square on 0 and on 1 degree of freedom as the number of languages grows (Self & Liang, 1987). With 8 to 12 languages the null puts 0.64 to 0.67 of its mass at zero, so the mixture is conservative. The power runs below use a simpler homogeneity test across languages (chi-square on L -1 degrees of freedom, size 0.043 to 0.051 under s = 0) and a t-test on per-language logits for the mean direction. CONDITIONAL on (D.2). Independent normal language effects on dimension scores are an assumption, not a result. Under (D.2) the language effects on a triad's three pairs are correlated, because they share dimensions, and additivity holds inside every language.

Rank one across languages. Languages can also be treated as columns in the D.4 table. A language whose order is a rescaled copy of English passes the rank test, and a language whose scores run opposite to English on every pair fails only the sign check. Proposition D.10 applies unchanged.

D.6 Power: how many directional items each test needs

All rows use power 0.80 at α = .05. Each test was also run with its null true, as a control that must reject near .05. The direction, triad, omnibus, rank-one and heterogeneity controls ran in the power simulations and rejected at 0.037 to 0.068. The mean-direction test across languages was not given a null run there.

An independent verification ran it, at 0.055 (8 languages, 100 items, s = 0.5) and 0.050 (4 languages, 50 items, s = 1.0) (deposit file wave1-math/p65_wave1_verify-run_2026-11-16.txt). Counts are independent directional items. The simulations anchor on the rounded share 0.74. The source value is 0.738. The corpus study's registered extension used a weighted stratified draw with a design effect of about 6 (5 to 7 by approximation), so its 155 directional items carried the information of about 22 to 31. Multiply by that factor if a future study draws the same way. A self-weighting draw of directional items keeps the factor near 1, apart from clustering by document. Direction counts are the smallest from which exact-binomial power stays at or above 0.80 for the next 20 counts (power is not monotone in the count, and the first count reaching 0.80 is 35, 49, 90 and 199 for shares 0.74, 0.70, 0.65 and 0.60). The half-chaining far share is 0.828, printed as 0.83. The triad count resolves an ordered triad, and catching a cycle is the separate power shown.

• Languages matter more than items per language. Once a language has about 100 time-place items, extra items barely move the mean-direction power. Extra languages do. Eight languages suffice if they differ by a logit standard deviation of 0.5. If they differ by 1.0, twelve languages give 0.90, and eight never reach 0.80 however many items each has.

• Per pair, not per language. About 300 directional items per language spread over 15 pairs is 20 per pair. That is enough for direction only on pairs with shares near 0.80. Each language needs at least 100 time-place items. The additivity test needs about 110 items per pair on each of a triad's three pairs. • Rare pairs. Pairs such as time-color may be rare in text. Proposition D.3 then applies: if some set of dimensions is stated under the rest but never over them, the estimate does not exist, and a dimension never compared leaves its score unidentified. One empty cell does not decide this. The whole win graph does. The six-dimension study counts the directional items per pair in a pilot before registering which triads enter F3. This is OPEN until that pilot runs.

• Coder error enters the likelihood. Estimate the flip rate from validation labels or from double-coded items outside the triad under test, under a stated error model, and fit with it (Proposition D.7). Ignoring it biases F3 toward the logical-dependence rival.

D.7 What changes for predictions F1 to F6

• F1 (direction per criterion) is unchanged and now carries sample sizes.

• F2 (transitivity) follows from any single scale (Proposition D.5), so it is a weak test. A failure would refute every scale model. Pooled data can cycle without any source cycling (Proposition D.8), so F2 is tested within criterion and language.

• F3 (additivity) is equivalent to Bradley-Terry (Proposition D.6). It is the sharp test of one scale against the pair-by-pair rival. Its failure rejects the Bradley-Terry scale under the pooling and coder-error assumptions, not an ordinal hierarchy, and coder error biases it toward the rival (Proposition D.7).

• F4 (convergence) splits into a rank test and a sign test (Propositions D.9, D.10). The current English data allow only the sign test, and that test does not reject convergence at .05, even under an exploratory one-sided reading.

• F5 (an empty "time changes over X" row) implies the scale estimate does not exist (Proposition D.3).

The registration needs a prior or a bias-reduced estimate, and a lower-bound report. The dictionary study's one falsifier puts an item in the row. However, three dimensions (size, intensity, quantity) are never stated over any other in the pooled matrix. The win graph is therefore not strongly connected, and the estimate still does not exist for the dictionary criterion.

• F6 (the registered strong form, share 0.80) is a statement about adjacent gaps of at least logit0.80 = 1.39 within each criterion. The English text gap is 1.04 (interval 0.25 to 2.12, from the source share 0.738, 0.561 to 0.893), so it neither reaches nor excludes 1.39.

Appendix A. Codebook v2 (five classes, decision steps, minimal pairs)

The unit is one sentence, read with the sentence before it. If a sentence holds more than one time-place pairing, the coder labels the one that is most clearly directional and notes the others. Navon (1978) claimed a hierarchy: time dominates space, and space dominates every other dimension. A hierarchy makes predictions about every pair of dimensions crossing his three levels (time, space, the rest; p. 224) and about how the pairs fit together. This appendix turns the claim into one model, says what the data can and cannot identify, derives when the hierarchy's two signature properties (transitivity and additivity) must hold, gives a test of whether Navon's criteria agree, extends the model across languages, and calculates the number of directional items each test needs. Verdicts use five words: PROVED, DISPROVED, CONDITIONAL, NUMERICAL EVIDENCE, OPEN. Every proof was checked in Wolfram Mathematica or by simulation, each with a control that fails when it should. Check labels such as W1 (Wolfram) and A1 (simulation) name lines of the output files in the deposit folder wave1-math/. An independent verification pass corrected the statement of Proposition D.3 and the design-effect figure in D.6.

Appendix D. A dominance scale for Navon's hierarchy

The core idea is simple. Give each dimension a single score. The larger the gap between two scores, the more often the higher dimension is stated over the lower one. If that picture is right, a handful of scores explains every pair, and the pairs must fit together in a specific way. If the pairs do not fit, no single score scale explains them.

Throughout, a directional item is a sentence, verb sense or experiment that puts one dimension over another (Appendix A gives the codebook). Items coded parallel or ambiguous are not directional.

D.1 The scale

Definition D.1 (dominance scale). Each dimension d (time, place, size, color, quantity, manner) has a score θ_d. For criterion c (Navon's change verbs, scope of markers, or the Garner interference test Navon cited) and dimensions i and j, the probability that a directional item puts i over j is P_c(i over j) = 1 / (1 + exp(-k_c (θ_i -θ_j))). (D.1)

In words: the share depends only on the gap between the two scores, through the logistic curve, and k_c says how sharply criterion c expresses dominance. Navon's hierarchy requires k_c > 0 for every criterion that expresses it. The fitted model lets k_c take either sign, so that a criterion stating lower-scored dimensions over

items putting the first over the second share = logistic(gap) text, scope criterion: time over place 0.738 (95% interval 0.561 to 0.893) interference experiments: time over space 14 of 39 (direction uncertain, p = .108; one scale would need a negative gap)The share follows the gap Intuition figure. Figure D1.

Figure D1. One scale with a score per dimension, and the share of directional items as a logistic function of the gap. Top: only the time-minus-place gap is measured (1.04 logit units with the scope criterion's sharpness set to 1, from the corpus study's registered extension). Other positions are illustrative. Bottom: the measured text share 0.738 (95% interval 0.561 to 0.893, shaded) on the curve, and the interference experiments' 14 of 39 directional experiments placing time over space, which the same scale could fit only with a negative gap, or equivalently a negative sharpness for that criterion (Section D.4). That point is not a second estimate of the same gap, and its own direction is uncertain (registered two-sided p = .108). Model figure, Appendix D.1.

pair should show Intuition figure. Appendix D.3, Wolfram checks W2, W4; 5% flip rate illustrative.

Figure D2.

Figure D2. Steps on the scale add on the log-odds scale, so two 0.80 steps predict 0.94 for the far pair, not 0.80. Left: logit0.80 = 1.386, and 1.386 +1.386 = 2.77, share 0.94, against the 0.80 that the no-chaining rival allows. Right: the far pair's share as a function of the two adjacent shares under one scale, under no chaining, and under one scale seen through a coder who flips 5% of directions, which bends the curve down. The solid blue curve (one scale) and the dashed orange line (no chaining) plot true shares. The dotted green curve plots observed far share against observed adjacent share after the flips, and it ends at 0.95, the largest share a 5% flip rate leaves. The dot marks the worked example of the left panel (0.80 on each step, 0.94 on the far pair). Appendix D.3 (Wolfram checks W2, W4). The 5% flip rate is illustrative.

Figure D3.

Figure D3. Pooling ordered sources, Proposition D.8. Each triangle has three dimensions i, j and k. An arrow points from the dimension stated over the other and carries its pooled share. (a) Two sources share the order i over j over k, with odds 9 and 1.1 per step, mixed 1 to 1 on every pair: the shares stay transitive, and the far pair's logit falls short of the sum of the two adjacent logits. (b) One order again, but the adjacent pairs draw on a sharp source and the far pair on a weak one (check A3a): weak transitivity holds and strong transitivity fails. (c) Three equal sources with the cyclic orders i over j over k, j over k over i, and k over i over j give two-thirds in each direction around the cycle (check A3b), exactly at the triangle bound of 1. The same two sources as in (a), weighted 9 to 1 on the adjacent pairs and 1 to 9 on the far pair, give 1.13 and cross it. Model figure, not data; every share follows from the source mixtures (checks A3a and A3b).
